en: Majjhima Nikāya 100:
Saṅgāravasutta.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Now at that time, a brahmin woman named Dhanañjānī was residing in Caṅcalikappa, having full confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
Then, while stumbling, the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī uttered this inspired exclamation three times:
“Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.”
Now at that time, a young brahmin named Saṅgārava was residing in Caṇḍalakappa;
he was a master of the three Vedas, including the glossaries and liturgical formulas, the phonology, and the histories as the fifth;
he was an expert in exegesis and grammar, and was proficient in Lokāyata philosophy and the marks of a Great Man.
The young brahmin Saṅgārava heard the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī speaking these words.
Having heard her, he said this to the brahmin woman Dhanañjānī:

"This brahmin woman Dhanañjānī has surely become estranged; this brahmin woman Dhanañjānī has surely become alienated from the brahmins who possess the threefold knowledge, yet she speaks in praise of that shaven-headed ascetic."
“But, dear sir, you do not know the virtue and wisdom of that Blessed One.
If, dear sir, you knew the virtue and wisdom of that Blessed One, you would not think that Blessed One should be reviled or abused.
“In that case, lady, when the ascetic Gotama arrives at Caṇḍalakappa, please inform me.”
“Yes, dear sir,” the brahmin lady Dhanañjānī replied to the young man Saṅgārava.
Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages through the Kosalans, arrived at Caṇḍalakappa.
There the Blessed One stayed in Caṇḍalakappa in the mango grove belonging to the brahmins of the Todeyya clan.
The brahmin lady Dhanañjānī heard: “It is said that the Blessed One has arrived at Caṇḍalakappa and is staying at Caṇḍalakappa in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins.
Then the brahmin lady Dhanañjānī approached the young brahmin Saṅgārava; having approached him, she said this to the young brahmin Saṅgārava:
“Dear sir, my good man, that Blessed One has arrived at Caṇḍalakappa and is staying at Caṇḍalakappa in the mango grove of the Todeyya brahmins.”
“Now then, dear gentle-faced one, do as you think fit.
“Very well, sir,” the young brahmin Saṅgārava replied to the brahmin lady Dhanañjānī. He then approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the young brahmin Saṅgārava said this to the Blessed One:

“Master Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have reached the perfection of mastery through direct knowledge regarding the present life, and they claim that this is the beginning of the holy life. Among them, Master Gotama, what is your position?

“Bhāradvāja, I say there is a distinction even among those who have reached the perfection of mastery through direct knowledge regarding the present life and who claim that this is the beginning of the holy life.”
There are, Bhāradvāja, some recluses and brahmins who rely on oral tradition.
Having reached the culmination and perfection of direct knowledge regarding the phenomena of this life through oral tradition, they claim to have attained the beginning of the holy life—
just like the brahmins of the threefold knowledge.
However, Bhāradvāja, there are some recluses and brahmins who, by mere faith alone, claim to have reached the perfection and consummation of direct knowledge regarding this present life,
and they profess the beginning of the holy life— just like those who rely on reasoning and investigation.

There are, Bhāradvāja, some recluses and brahmins who, having personally realized the Dhamma through direct knowledge regarding teachings unheard before, have reached the perfection and consummation of direct knowledge regarding this present life, and they profess the beginning of the holy life.

In this regard, Bhāradvāja, those ascetics and brahmins who, regarding teachings unheard of before, have through their own direct knowledge realized the Dhamma and attained perfection and mastery in the direct knowledge of the present life, and who profess the fundamental practice of the holy life—I am one among them.
And this, Bhāradvāja, should be understood by way of this method:

how those ascetics and brahmins, regarding teachings unheard of before, have through their own direct knowledge realized the Dhamma and attained perfection and mastery in the direct knowledge of the present life.
I am one among those who profess the fundamental holy life.
Here, Bhāradvāja, before my full enlightenment, while I was still an unenlightened bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me:
"The household life is cramped and a path of dust; going forth is like the open air."
"It is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life (brahmacariya) that is utterly complete, utterly pure, and polished like a conch shell.
What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Then, Bhāradvāja, after some time, while still young, with hair still very black and in the prime of youth, I...
Endowed with youth, I went forth from the home life into homelessness, shaving off my hair and beard and putting on saffron robes, even though my parents did not wish it and wept with tearful faces.
Having thus gone forth, seeking what is wholesome and searching for the supreme state of peace, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached him, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
‘Friend Kālāma, I wish to lead the holy life under this Dhamma and Discipline.
When this was said, Bhāradvāja, Āḷāra Kālāma said this to me:
‘May the venerable one stay here. I am staying here.’”
“Such is this Dhamma that a wise person, in no long time, having realized for himself through direct knowledge his own teacher’s doctrine, might enter upon it and dwell therein.
And so, Bhāradvāja, I soon and quickly mastered that Dhamma.

Yet, Bhāradvāja, with only that much—merely by striking my lips and merely by repeating what was said—I claimed to have the talk of knowledge and the talk of the elders, and I asserted: “I know, I see,” both myself and others.
Then, Bhāradvāja, it occurred to me:
“Āḷāra Kālāma does not proclaim that he has realized this Dhamma for himself through direct knowledge and dwells having attained it merely on the basis of faith alone;
surely Āḷāra Kālāma dwells knowing and seeing this Dhamma.”
Then, Bhāradvāja, I approached Āḷāra Kālāma. Having approached him, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
“To what extent, friend Kālāma, do you declare that you have dwelt having realized this Dhamma for yourself through direct knowledge and attained it?
When this was said, Bhāradvāja, Āḷāra Kālāma declared the sphere of nothingness.
Then, Bhāradvāja, it occurred to me:
‘It is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has faith, I too have faith;
it is not only Āḷāra Kālāma who has energy... [and so on]...’
There is mindfulness...
concentration...
wisdom; I too have wisdom.
‘What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Āḷāra Kālāma declares he has himself realized through direct higher knowledge and dwells having attained?
Then, Bhāradvāja, before long, I quickly realized that Dhamma myself through direct higher knowledge and dwelt having attained it.
Then, Bhāradvāja, I went to where Āḷāra Kālāma was, and having approached him, I said this to Āḷāra Kālāma:
“Friend Kālāma, is it to this extent that you have realized this Dhamma for yourself through direct higher knowledge, and having attained it, do you proclaim it?
“It is to this extent, friend, that I have realized this Dhamma for myself through direct higher knowledge, and having attained it, I proclaim it.
“Friend, it is to this extent that I too dwell having realized this Dhamma for myself through direct higher knowledge, and having attained it.”
“It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great fortune for us, friend,
that we see such a venerable co-practitioner as you. Thus,

that Dhamma which I have realized for myself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered upon it, and proclaim it— that very same Dhamma you dwell having realized for yourself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered upon it.”

The Dhamma that you have realized for yourself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered into it, is the very Dhamma that I have realized for myself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered into it, and now proclaim.
Thus, the Dhamma that I know, you know that same Dhamma; the Dhamma that you know, I know that same Dhamma.
Thus, as I am, so are you; as you are, so am I.
"Come now, friend, let us both, being tranquil, lead this community.
Thus, Bhāradvāja, Āḷāra Kālāma, though he was my teacher, placed me—his own pupil—in a position equal to himself, and honored me with great honor.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:
‘This Dhamma does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, nor to Nibbāna, but only as far as rebirth in the base of nothingness.
Then, Bhāradvāja, having found that Dhamma unsatisfactory, I became disillusioned with it and departed.
Then, Bhāradvāja, seeking what was wholesome and searching for the supreme state of sublime peace, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta. Having approached him, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta:
‘Friend, I wish to lead the holy life under this Dhamma and Discipline.
When this was said, Bhāradvāja, Udaka Rāmaputta said this to me:
‘May the venerable one stay. The Teacher has appeared for you as well.’”
“Such is this Dhamma that a wise person, in no long time, might realize for themselves through direct knowledge their own teacher’s doctrine and dwell having attained it.
And so, Bhāradvāja, I soon mastered that Dhamma quickly.

Yet, Bhāradvāja, with merely the flapping of my lips and mere prattle, I claimed: “I speak from knowledge; I know and see the doctrine of the elders,” and I made this claim both for myself and for others.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:
"Rāma did not proclaim that he had entered upon and dwelt in this Dhamma having realized it for himself through direct higher knowledge merely out of faith;
surely Rāma lived knowing and seeing this Dhamma."
Then, Bhāradvāja, I approached Udaka Rāmaputta and, having approached him, said this to Udaka Rāmaputta:
‘To what extent, friend, did Rāma declare: “Having realized this Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge, I enter upon and abide in it”?
When this was said, Bhāradvāja, Udaka Rāmaputta declared the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Then, Bhāradvāja, it occurred to me:
‘It was not only Rāma who had faith; I too have faith.
It was not only Rāma who had energy... [and so on].
There is mindfulness...
concentration...
wisdom; I too have wisdom.
‘What if I were to strive for the realization of that Dhamma which Rāma declared he had himself realized through direct knowledge, attained, and dwelt in?
Then, Bhāradvāja, before long, I quickly realized that Dhamma myself through direct knowledge, attained it, and dwelt in it.
Thereupon, Bhāradvāja, I went to where Udaka Rāmaputta was, and having approached him, I said this to Udaka Rāmaputta:
“Is it to this extent, friend, that Rāma declared this Dhamma after having realized it for himself through direct knowledge and attained it?
“It is to this extent, friend, that Rāma declared this Dhamma after having realized it for himself through direct knowledge and attained it.
“Friend, it is to this same extent that I too dwell having realized this Dhamma for myself through direct knowledge and attained it.”
“It is a gain for us, friend, it is a great blessing for us, friend,
that we see such a venerable co-practitioner as yourself. Thus,
that Dhamma which Rāma himself realized through direct knowledge, attained, and declared, you too dwell having realized that very Dhamma yourself through direct knowledge and having attained it.”

That Dhamma which you have realized for yourself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered into it, that same Dhamma Rāma has proclaimed, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, having attained and entered into it.
Thus, the Dhamma that Rāma directly knew, you know that Dhamma; the Dhamma that you know, Rāma directly knew that Dhamma.
In this way, as Rāma was, so are you; as you are, so was Rāma.
"Come now, friend, you yourself should lead this group.
Thus, Bhāradvāja, Udaka Rāmaputta, being my fellow celibate practitioner, placed me in the position of a teacher and honored me with great honor.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me:
‘This teaching does not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to awakening, nor to Nibbāna;
it leads only as far as rebirth in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Then, Bhāradvāja, having found that teaching unsatisfactory, I became disillusioned with it and departed.
Continuing my journey through Magadha in search of what is wholesome and seeking the supreme state of sublime peace, I eventually arrived at Uruvelā, the village of Senā.
There I saw a delightful stretch of land, a charming forest grove, and a river flowing with clear water, with beautiful landing-stairs, and lovely, with a village for alms nearby on all sides.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:

“Truly, this is a delightful stretch of land; it is a charming forest grove; there is a river flowing with clear water, with beautiful landing-stairs and lovely, and there is a village for alms nearby on all sides.”
“Sufficient indeed for a clansman seeking to strive is this for the sake of striving.
Then, Bhāradvāja, I sat down right there, thinking:
“This is sufficient for striving.”
Furthermore, Bhāradvāja, three similes occurred to me spontaneously, never heard before.

Suppose, Bhāradvāja, there were a wet, sappy piece of wood placed in water. Then a man would come along carrying a fire-drill, thinking: [...]"* *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the full simile continues with the man attempting to produce fire by rubbing the fire-drill against the wet wood, which is impossible because the wood is damp.*
‘I shall produce fire; I shall manifest heat.
What do you think, Bhāradvāja, would that man, taking an upper fire-stick and rubbing it against that wet, sap-filled piece of wood placed in water, produce fire and manifest heat?”
“No, Master Gotama.
And why is that? Because that log, Master Gotama, is wet and full of sap, and moreover it has been placed in water.”
“And furthermore, that man would only partake in exhaustion and distress.
“In the same way, Bhāradvāja, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell neither physically nor mentally withdrawn from sensual pleasures,
and whatever sensual desire, sensual affection, or sensual infatuation they have toward those pleasures— ”
If that thirst for sensual pleasures, that fever of sensual pleasures, has not been well abandoned and well stilled within them,
then even if those venerable recluses and brahmins experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted means,
they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed enlightenment. Even if those venerable recluses and brahmins do not [experience] such self-inflicted...
They experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, and they are incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
This, Bhāradvāja, was the first simile that occurred to me—extraordinary and never heard before.
Furthermore, Bhāradvāja, another second simile occurred to me—extraordinary and never heard before.
"Just as if, Bhāradvāja, there were a wet, sap-filled piece of wood placed far from water on dry land,
and then a man were to come along carrying an upper fire-stick,
thinking: 'I shall produce fire, I shall manifest heat.'"
“What do you think, Bhāradvāja, would that man,
taking an upper fire-stick and rubbing it against that fresh, moist piece of wood placed far from water on dry land, produce fire and manifest heat?
“Certainly not, Master Gotama.”
"And for what reason?
Because that wood, Master Gotama, is still wet and full of sap;
even though it has been placed far from water on dry land, that man would merely partake of exhaustion and frustration. "In the same way, Bhāradvāja..."
For whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell withdrawn from sensual pleasures both in body and mind,

yet their desire for sensual pleasures, their affection for sensual pleasures, their infatuation with sensual pleasures, their thirst for sensual pleasures, and their fever for sensual pleasures have not been thoroughly abandoned within themselves and have not been thoroughly stilled—
even if those worthy ones, the ascetics and brahmins, [practice] self-mortification...
They experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations; they are indeed incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

Even if those venerable recluses and brahmins do not experience self-inflicted painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations, they are still indeed incapable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
This, Bhāradvāja, was the second simile that occurred to me—extraordinary and unheard of before.
Furthermore, Bhāradvāja, a third simile occurred to me—extraordinary and unheard of before.
It is just as if, Bhāradvāja, there were a dry piece of wood, hollow and empty, lying far from water on dry land.
Then suppose a man were to come along carrying an upper fire-stick, thinking:
"I shall produce fire; I shall manifest heat.
What do you think, Bhāradvāja?
“Would that man, taking that dry wood and a fire-drill from a forest thicket placed far from water on dry land, and rubbing it with the upper drill-stick, produce fire and manifest heat?
“Yes, Master Gotama.
For what reason?”
“Indeed, Master Gotama, that firewood would be dry and withered, and moreover,
it would be placed far from water on dry land. “In the same way, Bhāradvāja, whatever ascetics or brahmins dwell withdrawn from sensual pleasures both in body and mind,
and whatever sensual desire, sensual affection, and sensual infatuation they have toward those sensual pleasures— ”
The thirst for sensual pleasures and the fever of sensual pleasures have been well-abandoned and well-calmed within him;
therefore, even if those venerable recluses and brahmins experience painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted means,
they are indeed capable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment— even if those venerable recluses and brahmins do not [experience] such self-inflicted...
"They experience feelings that are painful, sharp, harsh, and bitter, yet they are indeed capable of knowledge, vision, and unsurpassed enlightenment.
This, Bhāradvāja, was the third simile that occurred to me—extraordinary and unheard of before.
These three similes, Bhāradvāja, occurred to me, extraordinary and unheard of before."
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:
“What if I were to clench my teeth, press my tongue against the palate, and restrain, suppress, and torment the mind with the mind?
So, Bhāradvāja, I clenched my teeth, pressed my tongue against the palate, and restrained, suppressed, and tormented the mind with the mind.
Then, Bhāradvāja, as I clenched my teeth, pressed my tongue against the palate, and restrained, suppressed, and tormented my mind with my mind, sweat poured from my armpits.
It was just as if, Bhāradvāja, a strong man were to seize a weaker man by the head or by the shoulders and restrain, suppress, and torment him.
In the same way, Bhāradvāja, when I set my teeth against my teeth, pressed my tongue against the palate, and with my mind restrained, suppressed, and tormented the mind, sweat poured from my armpits.
Yet, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused;
nevertheless, my body was agitated and not calmed because I was so overcome by the exertion of that painful striving.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:
“What if I were to practice the meditation of breathlessness?
So, Bhāradvāja, I stopped the inhalation and exhalation through both my mouth and my nose.
"Bhāradvāja, when the inhalation and exhalation were stilled at my mouth and nose, there was an intense sound of air escaping through my ear canals.
Just as there is an intense sound from a blacksmith’s bellows being blown,
even so, Bhāradvāja, when the inhalation and exhalation were stilled at my mouth and nose, there was an intense sound of air escaping through my ear canals."
"But, Bhāradvāja, my energy was roused and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and unconfused;
yet my body was restless and unpacified because I was so intent upon that painful striving.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this thought occurred to me:"
‘What if I were to meditate on the breathless meditation?
Then, Bhāradvāja, I suppressed the inhalations and exhalations through my mouth, nose, and ears.
When the inhalations and exhalations were suppressed through my mouth, nose, and ears, Bhāradvāja, violent winds beat upon the top of my head.
"Just as, Bhāradvāja, a strong man might strike one on the head with a sharp-pointed spear,
even so, Bhāradvāja, when the inhalations and exhalations were obstructed at my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds churned within my head.
Yet, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unflagging, and my mindfulness was established and unconfused."
Moreover, my body was agitated and uncalmed, because I was still exerting myself with that same painful striving.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:
"What if I were to practice a meditation entirely without breath?"
So, Bhāradvāja, I stopped the inhalation and exhalation through my mouth, nose, and ears.
When the inhalation and exhalation were stopped through my mouth, nose, and ears, Bhāradvāja, there was an intense pain in my head.
It was as if, Bhāradvāja, a strong man were to bind a firm leather thong around my head as a headband.
In the same way, Bhāradvāja, when the inhalations and exhalations were obstructed through the mouth, the nose, and the ears, there was an extreme pain in my head.
Yet, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused;
however, my body was agitated and not calmed because I was so overcome by that exertion, being struck down by the effort.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:
“What if I were to practice the meditation of breathlessness?
So, Bhāradvāja, I stopped the inhalation and exhalation through my mouth, nose, and ears.
“Bhāradvāja, when the inhalations and exhalations were stilled through my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds cut through my belly. Bhāradvāja,
just as a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice might cut through a belly with a sharp butcher’s knife, even so, Bhāradvāja,
when the inhalations and exhalations were stilled through my mouth, nose, and ears, violent winds cut through my belly.”
“Moreover, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unconfused; yet my body was agitated and not calmed because I was so intent upon that painful striving.
Then, Bhāradvāja, it occurred to me:
‘What if I were to practice a meditation entirely without breath?’”
So, Bhāradvāja, I stopped the inhalation and exhalation through my mouth, nose, and ears.
When the inhalation and exhalation were stopped through my mouth, nose, and ears, Bhāradvāja, an intense burning arose in my body.
It was as if, Bhāradvāja, two strong men were to seize a weaker man by his various limbs and roast him over a pit of glowing embers, thoroughly scorching him.
In the same way, Bhāradvāja, when the inhalations and exhalations were obstructed through my mouth, nose, and ears, there was an intense burning in my body.
Yet, Bhāradvāja, my energy was aroused and unflagging, my mindfulness was established and unclouded;
nevertheless, my body was agitated and not calmed because I was so overcome by that exertion, being struck down by the effort.
Moreover, Bhāradvāja, when certain deities saw me, they said:
“The ascetic Gotama has passed away.
Some other deities said: [“He has not passed away”].
‘The ascetic Gotama has not passed away, but he is about to pass away.
Some deities spoke thus:
‘The ascetic Gotama has not passed away, nor is he about to pass away;’
“The ascetic Gotama is an arahant; such is the dwelling of an arahant.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:
“What if I were to practice the total cutting off of food?”
Then, Bhāradvāja, deities approached me and said this:
“Do not, dear sir, practice the total cutting off of food.
If you, dear sir, were to practice the total cutting off of food, we would infuse divine nutritive essence into you through your pores.”
‘With that you shall subsist.
Then, Bhāradvāja, it occurred to me:
‘If I were to claim total abstention from food, yet these deities were to infuse divine nutritive essence into my pores and I were to subsist on that;’”
‘That would be a falsehood for me.
Then, Bhāradvāja, I rejected those deities and said, ‘Enough!
It occurred to me, Bhāradvāja:

‘What if I were to take food little by little, drop by drop—whether it be mung-bean soup, or lentil soup, or pea soup, or vetch soup? Then, Bhāradvāja, I took food little by little, drop by drop—whether it be mung-bean soup, or lentil soup, or pea soup, or vetch soup. The Aggregate of Form in Terms of the Four Great Elements (Cātumahābhūtika Rūpakkhandha)
Whether it was bean soup, or lentil soup, or pea soup, or vetch soup, my body reached an extreme degree of emaciation.
Just as stalks of grass that are eighty days old or a hundred days old, even so did my limbs become through that very scantiness of food.
Just as a camel’s hoof, even so did my buttocks become through that very scantiness of food.
Just as a string of beads, even so my spine appeared with its vertebrae protruding and receding because of that very lack of food.
Just as the rafters of an old shed become sagging and decayed, even so my ribs became sagging and decayed because of that very lack of food.

Just as in a deep well the reflections of the stars appear deep down, sunken and hollow, even so in the sockets of my eyes the pupils appeared deep down, sunken and hollow because of that very lack of food.
Just as a bitter gourd, cut while raw, becomes withered and shriveled by the wind and sun, even so my scalp became withered and shriveled because of that very meager food.
Then, Bhāradvāja, when I intended to touch the skin of my belly, I would instead grasp my spine;
and when I intended to touch my spine, I would instead grasp the skin of my belly. To such an extent, Bhāradvāja, was I reduced.
Due to that very meagerness of food, my belly skin clung to my backbone.
Indeed, Bhāradvāja, when I intended to defecate or urinate, I would fall right there on my face due to that very meagerness of food.
And so, Bhāradvāja, while trying to comfort this body, I would rub my limbs with my hand. As for that...
Bhāradvāja, as I rubbed my limbs with my hand, the hairs fell from my body, rotten at the roots, because of that very meagreness of food.
Furthermore, Bhāradvāja, when people saw me, they said: “The ascetic Gotama is black.
Some people said: “The ascetic Gotama is not black; the ascetic Gotama is dark-complexioned.”
Some people said this: “The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor brown; the ascetic Gotama has a golden complexion.
To that extent, Bhāradvāja, my skin-color became so pure and bright, yet it was marred by that very lack of food.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:

‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past experienced painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted mortification, this was the utmost, there was nothing beyond this;

whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will experience painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted mortification, this will be the utmost, there will be nothing beyond this;
whatever ascetics or brahmins at present experience painful, racking, piercing, and bitter sensations resulting from self-inflicted mortification, this is the utmost, there is nothing beyond this.’
"Yet, by means of this bitter practice of self-mortification, I do not attain any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones.
Could there be another path to enlightenment?
This thought occurred to me, Bhāradvāja:
“I recall, however, that while sitting in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree in my father Sakka’s workplace,

secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.”
‘Could this indeed be the path to awakening?
Then, Bhāradvāja, a consciousness following after the memory occurred to me:
‘This very is the path to awakening.’
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:
"Why indeed am I afraid of that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states?
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:
‘I am not afraid of that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures and apart from unwholesome states.
Then, Bhāradvāja, this occurred to me:
‘It is not easy to attain such happiness with a body that has reached such an extreme limit.’
"What if I were to take solid food—rice and porridge?
Then, Bhāradvāja, I took solid food—rice and porridge.
At that time, Bhāradvāja, the group of five monks had attended upon me with this thought:
‘Whatever Dhamma the ascetic Gotama attains, he will declare it to us.
But when I, Bhāradvāja, began to take solid food—rice and gruel—those five bhikkhus of my group departed in disillusionment, thinking:
‘The ascetic Gotama has become luxurious; he has abandoned his striving and turned back to luxury.’
Then, Bhāradvāja, having taken solid food and regained strength, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...I entered and dwelt in the first jhāna.

With the subsiding of thought and examination, with internal tranquility and singleness of mind, without thought and examination, born of concentration, filled with rapture and happiness, I entered and dwelt in the second jhāna...
the third jhāna...
I entered and dwelt in the fourth jhāna.

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
I recollected my manifold past lives, that is: one birth, two births... [and so on] ...thus with their aspects and particulars, I recollected my manifold past lives.
This, Bhāradvāja, was the first true knowledge attained by me in the first watch of the night:
ignorance was dispelled, true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled, light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.

With my mind thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

“Then, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I saw beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—I understood how beings fare according to their kamma.
… [as before] … This, Bhāradvāja, was the second true knowledge attained by me in the middle watch of the night;
ignorance was dispelled and true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.”

When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
I directly knew, as it really is: "This is suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering";
I directly knew, as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; I directly knew, as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering."

I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’; I directly knew, as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’;
I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; I directly knew, as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’
I understood it as it truly is.
As I knew thus and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensual desire, my mind was liberated from the taint of existence, and my mind was liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: "It is liberated."
“I directly knew: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This, Bhāradvāja, was the third true knowledge attained by me in the final watch of the night;
ignorance was destroyed and true knowledge arose; darkness was dispelled and light arose, as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.”
When this was said, the young brahmin Saṅgārava addressed the Blessed One:
“The striving of Master Gotama has been steadfast; the striving of Master Gotama has been that of a true man, just as is the case for an Arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha.”
"But are there, Master Gotama, any gods?
"This is known to me by way of direct experience, Bhāradvāja:
namely, the 'super-gods'."
“Master Gotama, when asked, ‘Are there gods? you say, ‘This is known to me from a standpoint, Bhāradvāja, namely, that there are higher gods.
Is it not the case, Master Gotama, that if this were so, your statement would be empty and false?
“Bhāradvāja, when asked, ‘Are there gods? one might say, ‘There are gods,’ or one might say, ‘This is known to me from a standpoint.’”
“Now, in this matter, a wise person should reach a definitive conclusion on one side, namely:
‘There are deities.
But why did Master Gotama not explain it to me at the very outset?”
“Indeed, Bhāradvāja, it is highly esteemed in the world that ‘there are devas.
When this was said, the young brahmin Saṅgārava addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!

Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; [so has this been made clear by Master Gotama.]”
"In this very way, Master Gotama has proclaimed the Dhamma in many ways.
I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
The Saṅgāravasutta, the tenth, is finished.
The fifth chapter, the Brāhmaṇavagga, is finished.
Its summary verse (uddāna) is as follows:
Brahmāyu, Selassalāyana,
and the brahmin Ghoṭamukha;
Caṅkī and Dhanañjāni— among these, [he was the foremost].
Vāseṭṭha and Subhagārava.
This is the summary (uddāna) of the chapters: the chapter on the householder, the chapter on the bhikkhu, [the chapter on] Vāseṭṭha, and the chapter on Subhagārava.
The Paribbājaka, Nāma,
Rājavagga, and Brāhmaṇa—
these five are in the Majjhima Āgama.
The Middle Fifty has been completed.
